food.text: By about 1,000 BC, farmers in the Ma River and Red River floodplains had developed wet-rice cultivation. This farming led to the flourishing of Đông Sơn culture, which was notable for its bronze casting.

Cambodian cuisine draws on Khmer cuisine, a culinary tradition of the Khmer people that is nearly two thousand years old. Over the centuries it went on to absorb Indian, Chinese, French and Portuguese elements.
Around the 2nd century, Indian merchants introduced many spices to Khmer cuisine. Trade brought new flavors to the kitchens of the region.
A Chinese visitor around 400 AD noted the Indian influence on Khmer culture, cuisine included. This is an early outside record of Indian food ideas taking hold in the Khmer world.

The Silk Road, used from 130 BCE, ran from China and the Indonesian islands through India to the Middle East. Along it moved goods, diseases and ideas. Chinese and Indian merchants carried goods across it, with silks, rice and crockery coming from China and a plethora of influential spices from India.

Pandan is a tropical screwpine whose fragrant leaves flavor the cooking of Southeast Asia. It is a true cultigen believed to have been domesticated in ancient times, and being sterile, it reproduces only through suckers or cuttings.

Pandan was first described from specimens from the Maluku Islands. The rare presence of male flowers in those specimens may indicate that the islands are its origin, though no other wild specimens have been found, so this remains conjecture.

Cambodian anthropologist Ang Choulean says the influence of Indian cuisine on rural Cambodian cooking has been limited or even non-existent. Khmer royal cuisine, by contrast, adopted Indian-style curry pastes.

art.text: The Đông Sơn culture of North Vietnam flourished from about 1000 BC to the 4th century BC. It produced the world-famous Đông Sơn drums, a product of its advanced bronze-casting skills.
The Manunggul Jar was made in southern Palawan between 890 and 710 BC as a secondary burial jar. Its top cover depicts the journey of the soul into the afterlife, carried by a boat with a psychopomp.

Ancient Vietnamese cultural artifacts such as Dong Son drums have been found spread throughout Southeast Asia and South China. This suggests that ancient Viet (Yue) culture spread all the way south to Indonesia.
The Maitum anthropomorphic pottery was created in Cotabato between 5 BC and 225 AD. These secondary burial jars often depicted human heads, hands, feet and breasts.

Late in the Bronze Age in Vietnam, bronze made up more than 90 percent of tools and weapons. Exceptionally extravagant graves of powerful chieftains held some hundreds of ritual and personal bronze artifacts, including musical instruments, bucket-shaped ladles and ornament daggers.
In 100 BC the Kabayan Mummy Burial Caves were carved from a mountain in the Philippines, part of the same broad period of early Filipino art as the Manunggul and Maitum burial jars.

war.text: After the Han conquest of Nanyue in 111 BCE, much of Vietnam came under Chinese dominance for a thousand years. The long period was not quiet, though. It saw numerous uprisings, and Vietnamese kingdoms occasionally enjoyed de facto independence.

In February AD 40, the Trưng Sisters led a successful revolt against the Han governor Su Ding. They recaptured 65 states, including modern Guangxi. The revolt became one of the most famous uprisings against Chinese rule in Vietnamese history.

In 43 AD, Emperor Guangwu of Han sent his famous general Ma Yuan with a large army of 20,000 troops to crush the Trưng revolt. After a long, difficult campaign, Ma Yuan suppressed the uprising. The Trưng Sisters committed suicide to avoid capture.

In 207 BC, the former Qin general Zhao Tuo set up an independent kingdom on China's southern coast, in the Guangdong and Guangxi area. He called it Nam Việt, or Nanyue, to be ruled by the Zhao dynasty. He closed its borders, conquered neighboring districts and titled himself King of Nanyue.

In 179 BC, Zhao Tuo defeated King An Dương Vương and annexed the kingdom of Âu Lạc. It was a conquest by a former Qin general who had already made himself King of Nanyue. Âu Lạc was one of the indigenous chiefdoms that had emerged in the first millennium BCE.

Trưng Trắc led the revolt of AD 40 together with her sister Trưng Nhị. She was angered by the killing of her husband by the Han governor Su Ding. After the uprising succeeded, Trưng Trắc became the Queen, known as Trưng Nữ Vương.

Even though their revolt was crushed, the Trưng Sisters are still revered in Vietnam today. They are seen as the national symbol of Vietnamese women. Their story survives from a campaign that ended with a Han general's victory and their suicides.

literature.text: The first surviving literature in Vietnam is the Sanskrit Võ Cạnh inscription from the 4th century AD, found near Nha Trang. It belongs to either Funan or Chamic culture.

Chữ Hán, or Chinese characters, were introduced to Vietnam during the thousand years of Chinese rule from 111 BC to 939 AD. From 111 BC, Vietnamese literature was written in Văn ngôn, meaning Classical Chinese.
As Indic scripts were introduced from the Indian subcontinent, the people of Southeast Asia entered the historical period. They produced their earliest inscriptions around the 1st to 5th century CE.

Sanskrit inscriptions influenced Southeast Asia from the 4th century CE onward. Indic scripts adapted for Sanskrit appeared in Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia and Cambodia, where they evolved into local scripts such as Khmer, Javanese and Balinese.
The Sanskrit Võ Cạnh inscription near Nha Trang dates to the 4th century AD and is the first surviving literature in Vietnam. It belongs to either Funan or Chamic culture.
The Indianised Tarumanagara kingdom was established in West Java around the 400s. It produced inscriptions among the earliest in Indonesian history.
Indian scholars wrote about the Dwipantara or Jawa Dwipa Hindu kingdom in Java and Sumatra around 200 BC. It shows Southeast Asia appearing in Indian writings early.
India's earliest epic, the Ramayana, mentions Yawadvipa. Sugriva, the chief of Rama's army, dispatched his men to Yawadvipa, the island of Java, in search of Sita.

science.text: The Đông Sơn culture, a Bronze Age culture dating from approximately 1000 BCE to 100 CE, emerged in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam. It marked a high point in metallurgy and sophisticated bronze casting. It combined this with intensive wet-rice cultivation and advanced seafaring and shipbuilding techniques.

In Vietnam, bronze steadily displaced stone. By about 1000 BC it had replaced stone for about 40 percent of edged tools and weapons, rising to about 60 percent. Toward the end of the Bronze Age, bronze made up more than 90 percent of tools and weapons.

Đông Sơn bronze drums have elaborate geometric motifs and complex mathematical symmetry. Besides showing a sophisticated aesthetic sensibility, they reflect advanced control of furnace temperatures and mold-casting techniques.

Because Đông Sơn bronze casting was so prominent, people have sometimes wrongly assumed its inhabitants did not know iron smelting. Archaeologists have found iron weapons, tools and iron slag at Đông Sơn sites. At Gò Chiền Vậy in Hoài Đức, Hanoi, an iron hoe about 2,400 years old is direct evidence of ironworking.

Bronze in ancient Vietnam was not only for weapons, axes and ornaments. It was also made into sickles and other agricultural tools. The graves of powerful chieftains held some hundreds of ritual and personal bronze artifacts, including musical instruments, bucket-shaped ladles and ornament daggers.

politics.text: In 111 BCE the Han dynasty annexed the kingdom of Nanyue, and much of what is now northern and central Vietnam came under Chinese rule. Chinese control continued in various forms until 939 CE, when the Ngô dynasty was established. The period is known in Vietnamese as Bắc thuộc.

Around the early first century CE, Funan emerged on the lower Mekong as the first Indianized kingdom of Southeast Asia. It became a great economic power in the region. Its main city, Óc Eo, attracted merchants and craftsmen from China, India, and even Rome.

Through the formation of Indianized kingdoms, small indigenous polities led by petty chieftains were transformed into major kingdoms led by a Maharaja, with statecraft akin to India's. This process gave rise to Funan in southern Vietnam and Champa in south central Vietnam, among others.

The Trưng sisters rebelled against Han rule in 40 CE and set up an independent state at Mê Linh, at the center of the Red River Delta. Two years later the Han general Ma Yuan was called in from the northern frontier, where he had defeated the Xiongnu, to lead forces against them.

In 257 BCE the kingdom of Âu Lạc emerged as a union of the Âu Việt and the Lạc Việt, with Thục Phán proclaiming himself An Dương Vương. In 179 BCE it was defeated and annexed by Zhao Tuo, the ruler of Nanyue.

The idea of the "God King" and law codes modeled on Indian systems were embraced by numerous rulers of Southeast Asia. The Lin-I Dynasty of Vietnam adopted Sanskrit and dedicated sanctuaries to the Indian divinity Shiva. Many rulers saw themselves as reincarnations or descendants of Hindu gods.

Ma Yuan led over 2,000 ships and more than 20,000 warriors to strike at Douyang and Jiuzhen, where the remaining clan members of Trưng Trắc were located. The leaders of the Trưng rebellion were beheaded, and from Wugong to Jufeng he captured over 5,000 men. Afterward he created new commanderies and districts, organized town walls, dug irrigation canals, and made laws regarding the Yue people.

Zhao Tuo, a former Qin general, established an independent kingdom on China's southern coast in 207 BCE. He named it Nam Việt (Nanyue), to be ruled by the Zhao dynasty, and titled himself King of Nanyue. He also closed the borders and conquered neighboring districts.

In the latter half of the 4th century, a traveler named Yu Yiqi noted that central Vietnam was home to descendants of soldiers who had come with Ma Yuan three hundred years earlier. Originally only 10 households, they had intermarried and grown to 200 households, all named Ma.

philosophy.text: From around 500 BCE, expanding land and maritime trade carried Buddhist and Hindu beliefs into Southeast Asia's cosmology. By the early centuries of the common era, most of the principalities of Southeast Asia had absorbed defining aspects of Indian culture.

One of the earliest accounts of Buddhism in Southeast Asia describes a Theravada Buddhist mission sent by the Indian emperor Ashoka to modern-day Burma in 250 BCE. The Mon kingdom received the mission, and many people were converted.

Buddhism reached Southeast Asia both directly over sea from India and indirectly from Central Asia and China, in a process spanning most of the first millennium CE. It is thought to have entered through trade with India, China and Sri Lanka during the 1st, 2nd and 3rd centuries.

Buddhist monks and Hindu priests joined merchant classes to share their religious and cultural values. Indian religion was deeply absorbed by local cultures, which formed their own distinctive variations to reflect their own ideals.

Mahayana Buddhism is thought to have spread from both China and India into Southeast Asia during the first and second century. It took root primarily in maritime Southeast Asia, with a strong influence in Vietnam, partly due to its connection with China.

Hindu influences reached the Indonesian Archipelago as early as the first century. By the 4th century, the kingdoms of Kutai in East Kalimantan, Tarumanagara in West Java, and Holing (Kalingga) in Central Java were among the early Hindu states in the region.

Along the Mekong delta, communities labeled Funan show evidence of Indianized religious models. The earliest records engraved on a rock at Vocanh consist of Buddhist archives written in Sanskrit with south Indian scripts, dated to the early half of the third century.

The Indianised Tarumanagara kingdom was established in West Java around the 400s and produced some of the earliest inscriptions in Indonesian history. A marked Buddhist influence began in the region about 425.
Indian scholars wrote about a Hindu kingdom in Java and Sumatra around 200 BC. Yawadvipa, the island of Java, is mentioned in the Ramayana, where Sugriva dispatched his men there in search of Sita.

culture.text: By the early centuries of the common era, most principalities of Southeast Asia had absorbed defining aspects of Indian culture. Buddhist and Hindu beliefs spread through expanding land and maritime trade from around 500 BCE, and Buddhist monks and Hindu priests joined merchants to share their beliefs.

The Đông Sơn culture of northern Vietnam took its name from bronze drums first excavated in Thanh Hóa province in 1924. These kettledrums spread widely, and Đông Sơn artifacts have been found in places such as Malaysia, Laos and southern China. Vietnamese historians link the culture to the states of Văn Lang and Âu Lạc.

The Đông Sơn people were skilled at cultivating rice, keeping water buffalos and pigs, fishing, and sailing in long dugout canoes. They were also skilled bronze casters. Their drums are evidence of that craft.

The Sa Huỳnh culture of central and southern Vietnam cremated adults and buried them in lidded jars, a practice unique to the culture. The jar burials were usually accompanied by ritually broken offerings. The Sa Huỳnh people were most likely the predecessors of the Cham, founders of the kingdom of Champa.

Funan was a polity in the Mekong Delta region, and its name is known only from Chinese accounts, including those of the diplomats Kang Tai and Zhu Ying in the mid-3rd century CE. Funan is noted as the oldest Hindu culture in this region. Its language was an early form of Khmer, and its written form was Sanskrit.

Heger I type drums are identified by intricate decorations showing rings of warships and warriors in feather headdresses circling a sun at the center. Models of stylized frogs rest upon the sun. Heger II drums share the frogs and sun motif but are plainer and much bigger.

Sa Huỳnh people made distinctive ear ornaments featuring two-headed animals, which some believe depict saola. They were commonly made from jade (nephrite), but also from glass. Bead ornaments, most often of glass, were also common in Sa Huỳnh burials.

Óc Eo, a busy port of the kingdom of Funan in the Mekong Delta, may have been the port known to the Greeks and Romans as Cattigara. Its position on Southeast Asian sea routes made it a meeting place for craftsmen and traders. This brought foreign influences, notably from India.

Buddhism and Hinduism arrived in Vietnam by the 2nd century CE. This made Vietnam the first place to share influences of both Chinese and Indian cultures. Chinese rule began after the Han conquest of Nanyue in 111 BCE.

The Sa Huynh-Kalanay Interaction Sphere was a trade network linking Sa Huỳnh with the Philippines, Taiwan, Southern Thailand and northeastern Borneo. It is marked by shared red-slipped pottery and lingling-o ornaments. These were made from green jade sourced from Taiwan, green mica from Mindoro and black nephrite from Hà Tĩnh.

The Old Cham Đông Yên Châu inscription near Trà Kiệu dates from the late 4th century and was erected by King Bhadravarman I of Champa. It is written in Old Southern Brahmic script. It remains the oldest attested epigraph of any Southeast Asian language, predating Mon, Khmer and Malay by centuries.

The first evidence of writing in Vietnam came after the Han conquest of Nanyue in 111 BC, when Old Chinese and Classical Chinese were introduced. It survives only as short sentences engraved on bricks and coins. The first surviving literature is the Sanskrit Võ Cạnh inscription of the 4th century AD near Nha Trang.
